title: Switch
summary: Pick one path out of many with the switch statement and the switch expression.

steps.title: One value, many cases
body: A long `else if` chain that keeps comparing the **same** variable is hard to read. `switch` says it once: look at this value and jump to the matching `case`.
- Each `case` is a value to compare against. Only the first matching one runs.
- `break;` ends a case. C# will not compile a case that runs on into the next one.
- Two labels stacked with nothing between them (`"y"` and `"yes"`) share the same code.
- `default` runs when nothing matched. It is the `else` of a switch.

steps.explain: `case 2:` and `case 3:` are stacked, so both run the same code. Only one case ever runs, so `Other` is not printed.

steps.prompt: Complete the switch so `"red"` prints `Stop` and every other colour prints `Go`.
steps.explain: `case` names a value to match, `break` ends that case, and `default` catches everything else.

steps.title: Units to a timer
prompt: Read two lines: an amount (a whole number), then a unit letter. Using a `switch` **statement**, turn it into
seconds and print it with **your own** `Sk.FormatDuration` from *Numbers and math* (ready to call).
template: // Given: your earlier Sidekick pieces (the reference versions).
hints: Stack two labels to share code: `case "h":` then `case "H":`, then the line that prints.
Hours to seconds is `amount * 3600`; minutes to seconds is `amount * 60`.

steps.title: The switch expression
body: Very often a switch only exists to **choose a value**. The switch *expression* is a shorter form made for exactly that.
- The value comes **first**, then the word `switch`.
- Each line is an **arm**: `pattern => result`. No `case`, no `break`.
- `_` is the **discard**: it matches anything, like `default`.
- The whole thing produces a value, so it ends with `;` like any other assignment.

steps.prompt: Match each piece of syntax to its job.
pairs: matches anything, in a switch expression
matches anything, in a switch statement
separates a pattern from its result
ends a case in a switch statement
separates the arms of a switch expression

steps.title: Patterns: ranges and alternatives
body: An arm does not have to be a single value. It can be a **pattern** that describes many values.
- `< 13`, `>= 65` and friends compare the value, with the value itself left out.
- `and` requires both sides, `or` accepts either. Inside patterns you write the words, not `&&` and `||`.
Arms are tried **top to bottom** and the first match wins, exactly like `else if`. If an arm can never be reached because an earlier one already covers it, the compiler tells you.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines so 90 or more gives `"A"`, 70 to 89 gives `"B"`, and anything lower gives `"C"`.
steps.explain: The first matching arm wins, so the strictest test goes first. Put `>= 70` on top and the `>= 90` arm could never be reached, which is a compiler error.
`15 < 10` is false, so the first arm is skipped. `15 < 100` is true, so that arm wins and the `_` arm is never looked at.

steps.prompt: This switch expression has no `_` arm. What happens when `code` is `7`?
options: The program crashes with an exception when this line runs
steps.explain: A switch expression must produce a value. With no matching arm there is no value to give, so it throws. The compiler warns you about the gap; adding a `_` arm closes it.

steps.title: Seasons
prompt: Read a month number and print its season (northern hemisphere), using a `switch` **expression**.
No `if` allowed: let the patterns do the work.
hints: Winter is three separate values. Join them with `or`: `12 or 1 or 2 => "Winter"`.
A range needs both ends: `>= 3 and <= 5 => "Spring"`.
End with `_ => "Invalid month"` and remember the `;` after the closing brace.

steps.title: sk's command words
prompt: **Sidekick piece: how `sk` understands you.** `sk t`, `sk today` and plain `sk` must all mean `today`. Your code
becomes the body of `static string ResolveCommand(string word)`. `word` is given (whatever followed `sk`, maybe
with spaces or capitals). Trim it and make it lower case, then use a `switch` **expression** with `or` patterns
to put the command's real name in `result`:
| anything else | the cleaned word itself (so `Receipt` gives `receipt`) |
starter: // word is given. Put the command name in result.
template: Dojo.Eq("\"  ls \" means list", "list", ResolveCommand("  ls "));
hints: One arm per command, alternatives joined with `or`: `"" or "t" or "today" => "today",`
The last arm `_ => w,` hands back the cleaned word, and the expression ends with `};`.

build.title: Command aliases
build.unlocks: `sk t`, `sk ls`, `sk ?`: Sidekick now understands short commands.
transform: // Command aliases: your own passing code from the code-dojo C# track (Control flow > Switch).
